parsed.study_design: Historical-geographical institutional case study using regulatory statistics, documentary evidence, and industry interview evidence
parsed.population_and_sample: Domestic water consumers and the regulated water-supply sector in England and Wales; national regulatory and industry data, supplemented by industry interview evidence
parsed.exposure: Privatization, commercialization, economic and environmental regulation, competition policy, metering, and cost-reflective water pricing
parsed.outcome: Household water affordability and water poverty, metering coverage, consumer protection and exclusion risks, service pricing, and water-service and environmental quality
parsed.rationale: The sections “Market Environmentalism in Water Supply in England and Wales” and “The Drive for Commodification” document the post-1989 regulatory restructuring using sector statistics on investment, prices, water quality, and utility performance (pp. 548–552). “Metering Stymied” and “Repoliticizing Pricing” report access-relevant empirical outcomes, including over 99% network connection, domestic metering below 20%, water-poverty concerns, and protections for vulnerable consumers (pp. 557–559). Although analytically oriented, the article is an identifiable institutional case study with empirical regulatory, documentary, and interview evidence rather than purely doctrinal or normative commentary.
